claims.claim: A retirement account is an account designed to hold money for retirement, with tax advantages; tax-advantaged accounts are financial accounts that offer special tax benefits — such as pre-tax contributions, tax-deferred growth, or tax-free withdrawals — to encourage saving for purposes like retirement.

The tax idea: retirement accounts give contributions, growth, or withdrawals special tax treatment, with the benefit typically landing on the way in (pre-tax contributions, taxed withdrawals) or on the way out (after-tax contributions, generally tax-free qualified withdrawals); traditional and Roth 401(k) options both offer tax advantages, either now or in the future.

A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement plan that gives employees a choice of investment options; some employers match a portion of employee contributions, and the IRS confirms matching contributions are permitted if the plan document allows.

An IRA (individual retirement arrangement) is a tax-favored personal savings arrangement that allows you to set aside money for retirement; you can set one up yourself with a bank, insurance company, or other financial institution, choosing the vendor and investment options.

Mechanics: money goes in as contributions (often a slice of each paycheck), grows inside the account, and comes out as withdrawals in retirement; for traditional accounts, amounts including earnings generally are not taxed until distributed.
The law sets an annual limit on how much can be contributed to retirement accounts such as 401(k)s; specific dollar amounts change over time and are intentionally not stated in this lesson.

Taking money out of a retirement account before retirement age generally triggers an additional tax on the distribution — the early-withdrawal penalty; the lesson names the penalty generally without stating the rate.

Time matters: retirement money is long-term money that will not be used for decades, and retirement accounts are built to hold money across that span; the compound-growth mechanics belong to the sibling lesson.
Honest framing: a retirement account is a tax wrapper, not an investment; what is held inside the account — typically investments chosen from the plan's options — still carries risk.

conflictingEvidence: No conflicts among the sources used. The IRS and SEC Investor.gov describe the same general structure: tax-advantaged wrappers, traditional-vs-Roth timing, annual contribution limits, and an additional tax on early distributions. Contribution-limit dollar figures vary by year and plan type; the lesson therefore names the limits without numbers.
rightsIssues: All sources are U.S. government works (IRS, SEC Investor.gov). Facts restated in original prose; no source wording reproduced beyond short attributed phrases. usage REFERENCE_ONLY throughout.
